beliefs.practice: Create and reuse a single Motor/MongoClient instance for the whole process (singleton) and configure connection pooling (e.g., maxPoolSize=100) rather than creating a client per request.
Respect and implement Azure Cosmos/Mongo API rate limiting: on HTTP 429 responses read the Retry-After header and implement exponential backoff with jitter before retrying.

Use bulk unordered writes for ingestion (ordered=False / bulk_write with ordered=False or insert_many with ordered=False) and batch documents in sizes like 100–1000 to maximize throughput and avoid single-request timeouts.

Choose a partition key with high cardinality and even distribution (e.g., a hashed sender/sender_bic or a synthetic bucketed_date + sender) when creating the collection so writes and aggregations do not create hot partitions.

Index the fields used in your aggregation and query filters: at minimum create an index on message_date (or value_date) and a compound index on (message_type, message_date) to support daily group-by queries efficiently.
When creating indexes, prefer covering indexes for frequent queries (include fields used in match/sort/group) and inspect query plans (explain()) to verify the aggregation pipeline uses the index.

Respect Azure secrets best practices: do not store DOCUMENTDB_URI or keys in source or logs; load the connection string from environment variables or retrieve it at runtime from Azure Key Vault or another secret store.
Implement per-operation timeouts and serverSelectionTimeoutMS/ socketTimeoutMS on the client to avoid indefinite hangs (e.g., serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000, socketTimeoutMS appropriate for bulk ops).
Handle transient network or throttling errors explicitly in the ingestion loop: classify 429, network errors and 5xx as retryable and fail-fast for client errors (4xx other than 429).

Validate and enforce required fields in the application/ODM layer (Beanie Pydantic models) before sending documents to the DB to avoid partial/invalid writes; include explicit types for amounts and dates.
Avoid multi-document cross-partition transactions for high-throughput ingestion; if transactions are needed, design so they operate within a single partition key value.

For time-series/aggregation workloads, store both the full ISO timestamp (message_date) and a truncated date field (e.g., message_date_day as YYYY-MM-DD) you can group on — this makes daily aggregation efficient and indexable.
Expose aggregation endpoints that accept date ranges and message_type filters so aggregations can be bounded to a partitionable range; avoid scanning entire collection for daily summaries.
Monitor RU consumption and slow queries with Azure Metrics / Diagnostic Logs and adjust indexes or RU/cluster tier when bulk-ingesting to avoid RU throttling.

Use ordered=False and writeConcern w/ appropriate w and wtimeout only if you understand tradeoffs; for maximum throughput prefer lower synchronous write guarantees but ensure app-level validation/compensation for data loss.
If storing numeric amounts, store them as fixed-point (integer cents) or Decimal128 rather than float to avoid precision errors when summing totals in aggregation pipelines.
Keep parsers and validation idempotent: include a unique message_id and use upsert with a unique index on message_id to avoid duplicate ingestion from retries.
Limit document size to well under MongoDB/DocumentDB limits (e.g., < 16MB) — if you need large payloads store large blobs externally (e.g., Blob Storage) and keep references in the document.

For vector-capable clusters: store embeddings in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding) and create the platform-specific vector index (HNSW/IVF) per the provider’s index definition; keep embedding dimensionality and dtype consistent across documents.

Use explain() on the actual aggregation pipeline used by the endpoint (including group and $sum stages) to confirm indexes are used and to tune pipeline order (match → project → group → sort) for best performance.
Seed test data and run aggregation queries in a staging environment first; use the documentdb MCP/explain tools to verify created indexes and query plans rather than relying on assumptions.
Do not commit .env files containing secrets; commit a .env.example with placeholders and instruct operators to populate real credentials from Key Vault or environment injection.
Enable TLS/SSL for connections and validate server certificates when possible (use the driver default TLS mode) to protect credentials and PII in transit.
Design retention and archival strategy: use TTL indexes or scheduled jobs to move old messages to cheaper archive storage rather than retaining all documents in hot collection indefinitely.
Instrument request/ingest pipeline with tracing and metrics (requests/sec, errors, avg latency, bulk insert sizes, RU consumption, 429 counts) so production issues can be triaged quickly.
